description:
Former site of Banner Cottage, to the south of Hale Road, Speke. (1)
An estate plan of 1781 shows a house on this site. It is recorded as No. 32a, Banner Cottage and garden, part of No. 32, Walkers, which was occupied by Richard Walker. (2)
The building is shown on the estate plan of c.1825. (3)
No building is shown on the Tithe map of 1844 but the site is recorded as No. 349, a cottage and garden owned Richard Watt Esq. and occupied by Isaac Ireland. (4-5)
It is recorded as No. 47 Oglet Lane on the OS map of 1954.
It is last shown on the OS map of 1981; it does not appear on the OS map of 1992.

title: Farmhouse at Bannerigg Farm, Windermere
description:
Post Medieval farmhouse (main dwelling-house attached to a farm) recorded in The National Trust Sites and Monuments Record. The original house is located at the East end of the present building. The West end of the house was a former downhouse with cross-passage. The interior, however, largely dates to the 20th century when alterations, as well as an extension, were carried out.

Bannerigg Farm is 1 mile East of Windermere Station on the Kendal road. The main body of the house runs East to West with the original 'house' at the East end. This now forms Bedrooms 4 to 7, above the dining room (formerly firehouse with firehood and press cupboard) and the kitchen (former parlour and probably pantry). At the West end is the former downhouse with a cross-passage running North to South, now the entrance hall. This part of the building now contains the bathroom and Bedroom 3, above the playroom and lounge (perhaps a wash house in the 19th century). To the rear is a wing containing Bedrooms 1 and 2, above the rear sitting room and the staircase hall. This wing is of early 20th century date, possibly 1931 when the interior was altered by an architect or builder named Drewitt. Most of the internal fittings of the house are of 1931 or later. At the East end of the house is a lean-to brick structure of 20th century date with a utility room to its rear. The brief nature of this report is due to the utterly uncooperative attitude of the tenant. IMPORATANT FEATURES - Pree cupboard; beams and joists in dining room; roof structure over main house. WALLS 1. Main House - presumably slate rubble but roughcast throughout. Most windows presumably have timber lintels but these are hidden behind the render. Sills mainly concrete. 2. Rear wing - thin walls, ? brick or slate, rendered. 3. One-storied store room set an angle between Buildings 4 and 1 surface feathered slate walls laid in mortar. 4. Lean-to, 1-storey structure at East end of main house: South wall is slate rubble, the others rendered brick. Two porches with slate roofs with timber substructure, supported on softwood timber brackets. ROOF - Slate, with iron gutters and downspouts, sandstone ridges. Three chimneys, the central one (to main fireplace) is stone with a brick top, the other two roughcast with clay pots. 1. Main house - slate with Iron gutters and downspouts, sandstone ridges - the section over the main 'house' is older than that over the downhouse which is probably 19th or 20th century. 2. Rear Wing - slate, clay ridge riles, rendered stack with clay pots. WC Door - flush door, wooden handle, late 20th century. A chamfered door frame is visible on East wall. PLAYROOM - window - 4-lights, top opens as casement, early to mid-20th century. LOUNGE - This room was not seen. Windows - 4-light windows, one at top opens as fanlight, mid-20th century. Other not seen. Corner fireplace suggests that room may once have been a wash house. DINING ROOM (former firehouse) - Door - plank door, three battens, countersunk hinges, Iron lock, 20th century. Windows - 1. firewindow, four fixed lights, 20th century. 2. 8-lights, 20th century. Fireplace tiled, 20th century, in largely black chimney breast. Press Cupboard in East wall, 'GWA 1673' (George and Agnes Williamson), of three stages under overhanging cornice with drops at either end. 1. Top stage as twp decorated doors on either side of central carved panel, butterfly and arrowhead hinges, lower right one has been repaired, guilloche carving round panels. 2. Middle stage has plain moulded doors on either side of central panel, right hand door knob missing and replaced by wooden catch, right hand hinges both repaired. 3. Lowest stage had central panelled door with wooden knob between two fixed panels. All stands on a plain plinth. Permission to photograph the cupboard was refused by the tenant. Beams - 1. in fact two beams side by side, one probably to support the firehood and the other the floor above, adzed hardwood, North to South, resting on the heck to the West end, 17th century. 2. Beam over door is chamfered hardwood, 17th century, with shallow arch cut into it. Chamfered joists with run-off stops. KITCHEN - Doors - 1. flush door, unpainted, late 20th century. 2. flush door but four battens on pantry side, Aluminium latch. Window - 1. Six lights, early 20th century, 2. Three lights, one fixed, one opens as casement, one opens as fanlight, late 20th century. PANTRY - Door - 1. Nine and a half planks, four battens, strap hinges, Iron lock. 2. flush door, Aluminium latch. Window - 3-light as kitchen. Floor concrete. UTILITY ROOM 1 - Door - five and a half planks, sliding, reused. WIndow - 2-lights, top opens as fanlight. Floor concrete. title: High Barn, former house converted, Bannerigg Farm, Windermere
description:
Converted farmhouse (main dwelling-house attached to a farm), now used as a barn (building used primarily for storing hay, grain, farm equipment or as a shelter for livestock) and cow house (building in which cattle are housed overnight), recorded by The National Trust Sites and Monuments Record. The building is thought to be Post Medieval, though has undergone a number of alterations since.

This former house stands to the North of Building *1 and forms one side of an L-shape together with building *4. It is 3-bays long with a first floor loft (formerly bedrooms) with the remains of a smoke-hood at the West end. This floor is reached by an external flight of slate steps of 18th or 19th century date. Below is a mid-20th century concrete shippon, formerly divided with firehouse at West end with a gable entry, now blocked, and parlour and pantry at East end. The pantry would have been at the North side and the parlour at the South end. IMPORTANT FEATURES - Roof structure; remains of smoke-hood; beams supporting first floor; remains of plaster on walls of first floor including beaded edges to window reveals. WALLS - Surfce gathered slate laid in mortar with uneven quoins. Hardwood timber lintels to all openings. Those on the ground floor have slate drip-courses above. On the North wall at the junction with building *4 there is no joint. The walls have presumably been partially rebuilt and joined. External slate steps with iron railins to first floor on the South wall. Various blocked openings, including two on the first floor North wall and two on the ground floor South wall. Massive cobbles in lower courses of South wall at East end. ROOF - Slate-covered with clay ridge and cast Iron gutter. Three bays long, two tie-beam trusses with collars, each notched and pegged twice at the apex. Collars pegged once to principal rafters, and tie beams twice. Most members are chamfered. Two through purlins on each pitch. All this is reused hardwood. The tie-beam for the East truss is a reused purlin for a wind-braced roof with mortice and pegholes for wind-braces, and has various pieces of applied timber including a piece of oak boarding. The tie-beam for the West truss is a reused cruck blade with mortice holes for collar and tie beam. The bottom purlin on the North pitch, centre bay, is also a reused cruck. The remaining purlins are probably reused from a cruck building. The roof was possibly reconstructed in the second half of the 17th century. The principal rafters have red lines on the undersides like those at Grove Cottage and Mislet farmhouse. Rafters all sawn softwood as is the ridge purlin which is laid upright, torched, late 19th century. LOFT (former bedrooms) Door - originally three Oak planks, three battens, all moulded, central plank was two panels, late 17th or ?early 18th century; drop-on strap hinges, Iron bold, two added planks, 20th century. Windows - 1. Four lights, mullion and transom, chamfered members, all fixed, reused, mid- to late 19th century. 2. Nine fixed lights, late 19th or 20th century. 3. Missing. Two blocked window openings on North wall have remaining plaster beading to the reveals. Chimney hood has two corbelled beams remaining at the head, but the stack above was removed when the building was reroofed. The impression of the hood remains in the plaster on the wall, very vertical. Quite a lot of plaster remains on the walls. GROUND FLOOR SHIPPON - Shippon stalls for eight cows, cement walls and concrete divisions, now with Iron gates and rails to form loose boxes, late 20th century. Six chamfered beams, the four westernmost covered with hardboard but probably hardwood; two easternmost are soft wood, 20th century; westernmost is corbelled onto the wall and was probably the firebeam. Joists and floorboards above are sawn softwood, 20th century. Floor concrete, dug out when concreted. Door - bottom half of stable door, seven planks, three battens, drop-on hinges, remains of bolt, 19th century. Windows - 1, 2 and 3 - Six lights, bottom three fixed, top three open as hopper, mid-20th century, 4. formerly eight lights, bottom four fixed, top four missing but opened as hopper, mid-20th century. 5. formerly a door, now as windows 1, 2, and 3. (NT Vernacular Buildings Surveyor, 1988).

title: Bank barn at Bannerigg Farm, Windermere
description:
Bank barn building with first floor level threshing floor (barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor) above cow house accommodation (building in which cattle are housed overnight) and storerooms. The current arrangement of the Post Medieval building is of the 19th or 20th century, though a number of openings survive include an owl hole.

This barn stands to the East of building *1 and has a barn (?originally with threshing floor - no sign of a winnowing door now visible, perhaps due to rebuilding of West wall), above is a shippon and three storage rooms. The ground floor arrangement is mid- to late 20th century. At the North end on ground floor level is a lean-to open store of 19th or 20th century date. On the East side at first floor level is a lean-to open store of breeze block and corrugated Iron of the late 20th century. IMPORTANT FEATURES - Roof structure; 19th century shippon stalls on ground floor. WALLS - Rubble slate, mainly surface-gathered with long uneven horizontal quoins. The South gable has a profusion of drip-courses and an owl hole. The West wall has slate drip-course over the ground floor window and door openings which have hardwood lintels. The North wall has various ventilation holes and an owl hole. Both West and East walls appear to have been rebuilt at first floor level. ROOF - Slate covered, sandstone ridge and cast Iron gutters. 3 bays long, two tie-beam trusses with collars pegged once to principal rafters; tie beams pegged twice to principal rafters. Two through purlins on each pitch, diamond set ridge purlin. All this timber is hardwood, possibly Ash. Rafters are sawn softwood, torched, late 19th century. INTERIOR SHIPPON - has six stalls with chamfered Pine frames with run-off stops and Pine boarded partitions within, mid- to late 19th century. Door - Six planks, three battens, drop-on hinges, Iron bolt, late 20th century in chamfered frame with three lights above the door, late 19th or early 20th century. Pine beams, Pine joists and planked to floor above. Floor concrete. STORES 1 AND 2 - Door - sliding door, six chamfered planks in a frame, two battens, 20th century. Windows - Three-lights, two fixed, centre one opens as hopper, 20th century. One light, hopper, mid- to late 20th century. Beams and joists as in shippon. Breeze-block partition North to South down centre. Floor concrete. STORE 3 - Door - Five planks within a frame, the bottom half of a stable door, drop-on hinges Iron bolt, late 19th century. Beams and joists as in shippon. Floor concrete. FIRST FLOOR - divided by corrugated Iron partition under South tie-beam. Door - wain doors, each seven planks, three battens and one added batten, drop-on arrowhead hinges, Pine, late 19th or early 20th century; lintel is reused hardwood. Floor - 7" Pine boards. OPEN STORE 1 - to East, corrugated Iron and breeze blocks, late 20th century. OPEN STORE 2 - to North, corrugated Iron, roof supported on two softwood beams and at the front on a reused hardwood beam. (NT Vernacular Buildings Surveyor, 1988).

title: Threshing barn at Bannerigg Farm, Windermere
description:
Threshing barn (barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor) recorded by The National Trust Sites and Monuments Record. The building overlies the filled in remains of a 17th century house. The building is Post Medieval, but has renewed guttering and roofing in places.

This building forms an L-shape with Building *5. It is a 6-bay threshing barn, of which the southern three bays are built upon the partially filled in remains of a 17th century house. There is a threshing floor in the third bay from the North. Two blocked windows of the former house are to be seen under a slate drip-course on the West wall of the building at the South end. IMPORTANT FEATURES - roof structure; 17th century window frame in West wall. WALLS - Mostly surface gathered slate rubble. The South gable has four slate drip-courses and a blocked owl hole. At the South end of the West wall is a drip-course which indicates the first floor level of the former house with two blocked windows beneath, each with a hardwood lintel. At the North end of the West wall are two other blocked openings with slate-hung hardwood lintels and slate drip courses, this time belonging to the barn. The winnowing door also has a slate hung hardwood lintel. The wain doors are protected by a pentice roof covered with corrugated Iron, of 20th century date. ROOF - Covered with local slates, clay ridge, cast Iron and plastic gutters. Six bays, with five tie-beam trusses with collars, each collar pegged once to the principal rafters; the principal rafters are notched and pegged twice at the apex. Two through purlins on each pitch. Sawn softwood ridge purlin formerly a diamond set purlin. Rafters are all sawn softwood, torched, 19th century. Much of the roof structure is re-used timber. INTERIOR - Four loose boxes with iron gates and divided by breeze block partitions covered in cement. Floor - concrete. (NT Vernacular Buildings Surveyor, 1988).

title: Hayloft above Loose Boxes, Bannerigg Farm, Windermere
description:
A hayloft (a loft over a stable or barn used for storing hay) of post medieval date.

This building stands to the South of building *1. It is 2-storeys high and although formerly a house bears few traces of this because of considerable reconstruction in the late 19th century. It comprises a hayloft above a collection of loose boxes, and has a lean-to loose box on the South side. On the North wall there are traces of a pitched roof at right angles to the main building, perhaps for a former porch. The building has been extended to the West by about 1m. WALLS - Surface-gathered and quarried stone. Opening altered on all walls. West gable appears to have been rebuilt in the 20th century, and East gable also rebuilt. There are hardwood lintels to openings on the North wall and East gable, and a blocked vent on the first floor of the South wall. The lean-to loose box is also built of surface gathered and quarried slate. ROOF - Slate covered with clay ridge and cast Iron gutter. Structure not seen, but probably 3-bays long with two roof trusses and one through purlin on each pitch. The lean-to has a softwood roof structure. INTERIOR - Breeze block partitions for loose boxes, softwood gates and uprights, late 19th or early 20th century. Ground floor has brick floor; upper floor not seen but beams, joists and floorboards visible (S3172).

title: John Bannerman
description:
Archaeological remains associated with the loss of this vessel are not confirmed as present at this location, but may be in the vicinity (see also NPRN 506814).

Event and Historical Information:
The JOHN BANNERMAN was a wooden full-rigged ship built William and Richard Wright at St John, Newfoundland, in 1854. Technical and configuration specifications are given as 1201gt, 1131nt (or 1132gt sources differ); 180ft length x 33ft breadth x 22ft depth; 3 masts; hull constructed of spruce and sheathed in felt and yellow metal, partly fastened with iron bolts. At time of loss, the vessel was owned by its builders William and Richard Wright (Tams Shipbuilding Co) and two merchants also from St John, James and Robert Reed. The JOHN BANNERMAN was carrying 3500 bales of cotton to Liverpool when it drove ashore at Porth y Post, Penrhos Feilw, on 2 March 1855. A southwesterly force 7 gale was blowing. Six of the 26 crewmembers attempted to reach the shore in one of the ship's boats, but the boat was never seen again. During the night, the vessel became much damaged and about 8 on Sunday morning broke up and since become a total wreck. The ship's cargo of cotton came ashore and local newspapers reported that the coast looked like it had a carpet of snow 2-3ft thick. The ship's St John's registry was closed in 1855. However, it is possible that the hull was salvaged and rebuilt, as the vessel's name reappears in Lloyd's Register from 1858 onwards.

Sources include:
Caernarfon and Denbigh Herald, 10 March 1855 
Larn and Larn Shipwreck Database 2002
Lloyds Register of British and Foreign Shipping, 1 July 1854 - 30 June 1855, number 24 in J
Memorial University of New Foundland, 1998, Ships and Seafarers of Atlantic Canada CD ROM

Maritime Officer, RCAHMW, October 2009.
